"""A surface-level guess at layers.15.mlp.down_proj:4032, one MLP unit of layer 15.

This unit is mostly quiet and only weakly tied to the text. Its clearest high values sit on
words inside section headings: markdown lines that start with '#', ALL-CAPS words, and short
title-like lines with no sentence punctuation ("BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION", "## Java").
Code import and package lines push it slightly negative. The program predicts a small value
from those four cues and a small baseline elsewhere. It explains very little variance (well
under 1%); the unit's spikes depend on context this program does not read.
"""

READS = ()
BASE = 0.02
HEADING = 0.3  # the line starts with '#'
UPPER = 0.25  # this token is an ALL-CAPS word
TITLE = 0.03  # short line with no sentence punctuation
CODE = -0.05  # line is an import / package / namespace line
PUNCT = set(".,;:!?")


def _line(prefix):
    """The text of the current line up to and including this token, same document only."""
    parts = []
    docs = prefix.document_ids
    for j in range(len(prefix.token_strings) - 1, -1, -1):
        if docs[j] != docs[-1]:
            break
        s = prefix.token_strings[j]
        if "\n" in s:
            parts.append(s.split("\n")[-1])
            break
        parts.append(s)
    return "".join(reversed(parts))


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    line = _line(prefix)
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip()
    value = BASE
    if line.lstrip().startswith("#"):
        value += HEADING
    if token.isupper() and token.isalpha():
        value += UPPER
    if len(line) <= 60 and not set(line) & PUNCT:
        value += TITLE
    if any(word in line for word in ("import ", "package ", "namespace ")):
        value += CODE
    return carry, value

"""Explainer for layers.15.mlp.down_proj:4033.

What it does, in plain terms: this component mostly lights up on the NUL byte
(the token "\\x00") in text that is stored as UTF-16: every letter is followed
by a NUL, so the NULs come every other token. On those NULs it writes a large
value (about 13), and about 3 when the NUL follows a space. Weaker, smaller
responses come from a few other kinds of token: periods that end a short
capitalised abbreviation ("Dist.", "Rep.", "Supp.", "Id."), code and LaTeX
punctuation (backslash, backtick, quotes, braces), and runs of indentation
spaces. Everything else sits near zero.

The values are the mean activation of each class over 20,000 training rows.
The program only reads the current token and the one before it.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

NUL = b"\x00"
CODE_TOKENS = {
    "\\", " \\", "`", '"', "'", '":', '",', "',", "`,", "{", "}", "}}", "\\n", '\\"',
}
NUL_AFTER_LETTER = 13.4
NUL_AFTER_SPACE = 3.4
ABBREVIATION_DOT = 1.25
OTHER_DOT = 0.15
CODE_PUNCTUATION = 1.0
INDENT_RUN = 0.3


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    same_doc = len(prefix.token_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip() if same_doc else None

    if prefix.token_bytes[-1] == NUL:
        # NUL after a space (the interleaved space in UTF-16 text) is weaker.
        return carry, (NUL_AFTER_SPACE if prev == "" else NUL_AFTER_LETTER)
    if tok == ".":
        if prev and prev.isalpha() and len(prev) <= 3 and prev[0].isupper():
            return carry, ABBREVIATION_DOT
        return carry, OTHER_DOT
    if tok.strip() == "" and len(tok) >= 2:
        return carry, INDENT_RUN
    if tok in CODE_TOKENS:
        return carry, CODE_PUNCTUATION
    return carry, 0.0

"""Distinctness detector for layers.15.mlp.down_proj, component 4034.

What it responds to: words that say things are distinct, different, unique or unequal
("distinct", "≠", "unique", "different", "orthogonal", "disjoint", "differ", ...). The
component fires on those words, most strongly when they sit in a constraint such as
"must be different", "all ... distinct", "no two ... the same". It is quiet on almost
everything else.

What this program does: on a trigger word it predicts that word's typical activation;
if a constraint cue (must, all, no, two, same, not, be, ...) occurs among the 8 tokens
before it, in the same document, it adds a boost. Every other token gets the component's
usual resting value. Honest limit: this captures only a small part of the variance.
Most of the component's large activations occur on ordinary words inside
distinctness/constraint sentences, which a word list does not reach.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# Typical activation on each word of distinctness (measured on training text).
TRIGGER = {
    "distinct": 4.4,
    "≠": 3.8,
    "!=": 0.3,
    "distinctive": 2.6,
    "orthogonal": 2.4,
    "disjoint": 2.4,
    "uniqueness": 2.2,
    "unique": 1.7,
    "uniquely": 1.5,
    "varying": 1.5,
    "distinguish": 1.3,
    "differ": 1.0,
    "different": 0.9,
    "independent": 0.8,
    "divers": 1.9,
}
# Words that, shortly before a trigger, mark a constraint about sameness or distinctness.
CUE = {"must", "should", "all", "each", "no", "two", "same", "adjacent", "not", "cannot",
       "be", "distinct", "unique"}
RESTING = -0.04  # the component's usual value on ordinary tokens
BOOST = 3.0  # added to a trigger that follows a constraint cue


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    doc = prefix.document_ids
    t = prefix.position
    word = prefix.token_strings[t].strip().lower()
    value = RESTING
    if word in TRIGGER:
        value = TRIGGER[word]
        recent = [prefix.token_strings[j].strip().lower()
                  for j in range(max(0, t - 8), t) if doc[j] == doc[t]]
        if any(w in CUE for w in recent):
            value += BOOST
    return carry, float(value)

"""Layer 15 MLP, component 4035: a diffuse, context-driven signal with no simple concept.

Its read direction is mostly layer 15's MLP hidden unit 4035 (about 30% of its squared
norm; the component's activation correlates 0.43 with that unit), and its write direction
is close to that unit's down-projection column (cosine 0.8).

What I measured on about 8k training rows, to find a concept behind it:
- Token identity explains nothing on held-out rows (a per-token mean table: R^2 < 0).
- Single token categories (digit, space-led, code symbol, non-ASCII, newline, capitalised)
  explain under 0.1% of its variance; a linear fit on windowed category counts, 0.14%.
- Position in the document, repetition, and document means explain under 3%.
- Its one clear regularity: the first token of a document reads as about 0.

So the program predicts 0 at each document's first token, and the component's average
value (about -0.024) everywhere else. This is a baseline, not an explanation of its
behaviour: the largest activations (+4.6, -4.4) occur mid-phrase in mixed text, code and
other languages, with no common trigger I could name.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = -0.024


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    t = prefix.position
    starts_document = t == 0 or prefix.document_ids[t] != prefix.document_ids[t - 1]
    return carry, 0.0 if starts_document else MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Opening parentheses that start an aside after a name or a term.

This component is silent on almost every token. Its large responses are on an
opening parenthesis, " (" or "（", that follows a name or a term in running
prose: "Anthony Browne (", "University of Southern California (", "Environmental
Protection Agency (EPA)". There it is strongly negative, most negative when the
parenthesis comes right after a capitalised name and is the first parenthesis in
its document. After code, maths or an operator, where "(" is a call or grouping,
it is near zero or slightly positive.

The program predicts 0 on every token except an opening parenthesis. There it
reads the token just before: code-like (operators, brackets, if/for/return),
a capitalised name, another word, or anything else. It then sets a base level
for that kind, and moves it up as the document has already opened more
parentheses (the first one is the most negative).
"""

import math
import re

READS = ()

OPEN_PARENS = {" (", "（"}
CODE_CHARS = re.compile(r"[=+*/{}<>|&;\\\[\]]")
CODE_WORDS = {"if", "for", "while", "return", "func", "catch"}
LETTERS = re.compile(r"[^\W\d_]+")

# Level at the first parenthesis of a document, per kind of token before it.
LEVEL = {"code": -0.65, "name": -4.8, "word": -4.1, "other": -3.2}
# Change per unit of log(1 + parentheses already opened in this document).
SLOPE = 0.85


def before_kind(text):
    """Classify the token before the parenthesis."""
    s = text.strip()
    if CODE_CHARS.search(s) or s in CODE_WORDS:
        return "code"
    if LETTERS.fullmatch(s):
        return "name" if s[0].isupper() else "word"
    return "other"


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    count = carry[1] if carry is not None and carry[0] == doc else 0
    if prefix.token_strings[-1] not in OPEN_PARENS:
        return (doc, count), 0.0
    before = prefix.token_strings[-2] if len(prefix.token_strings) > 1 else ""
    value = LEVEL[before_kind(before)] + SLOPE * math.log1p(count)
    return (doc, count + 1), value

"""Component p-82af68dd@100000/layers.15.mlp.down_proj:4037.

Its activation is, to a very good approximation, the MLP hidden unit 4037 of layer 15
(about 60% of its input direction is that one unit), so it is a single neuron's readout.

What it does, as far as a readable rule goes: it sits near a small positive baseline on
most tokens, and it is pushed clearly negative on words that open a time, condition,
or concession phrase ("when", "whenever", "wherever", "regardless", "depending",
"despite", "during", "if", "over", "since", "given", "where", ...). "when" and
"regardless" are among the strongest. The program predicts the baseline for every other
token, and the listed value for these words. It keeps no state and reads only the newest
token.

Limits: these words are rare and the neuron's spread is mostly on ordinary tokens, whose
values depend on context that no word list captures. A full token-by-token lookup
explains only about 2-3% of the variance on held-out text, so this program explains about
1%. Its end-to-end effect on the model is close to switching the component off.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

BASELINE = 0.05
"""The activation's typical value on ordinary tokens (its mean is about 0.047)."""

# Words that open a time, condition, or concession phrase, with their typical activation.
SUBORDINATORS = {
    "wherever": -4.0,
    "regardless": -2.5,
    "depending": -2.4,
    "whenever": -1.7,
    "despite": -1.3,
    "throughout": -1.3,
    "when": -1.15,
    "whatever": -1.0,
    "across": -0.8,
    "during": -0.5,
    "though": -0.5,
    "once": -0.5,
    "until": -0.45,
    "based": -0.45,
    "every": -0.4,
    "unless": -0.4,
    "if": -0.4,
    "over": -0.4,
    "given": -0.35,
    "where": -0.3,
    "within": -0.3,
    "since": -0.25,
    "while": -0.15,
    "as": -0.15,
    "after": -0.15,
    "whether": -0.2,
}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    """The activation at the newest token: a listed word's value, else the baseline."""
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    return carry, float(SUBORDINATORS.get(word, BASELINE))

"""Layer 15 MLP down-projection component 4039: a near-silent, text-unpredictable direction.

What it does: it writes a tiny, roughly zero-mean signal into the residual stream
(its activation has mean about 0.04 and standard deviation about 0.38, with both signs).
Its activation is a linear read of the layer-15 MLP hidden state (mostly hidden unit 4039),
and that hidden state depends on the whole context in ways no short rule over the tokens
captures: a lookup of the current token, the previous token, the token's character class,
or its position in the document explains almost none of its variance on held-out text.

So this program predicts the component's typical value everywhere, its mean, and nothing
more. Predicting the mean is the best constant under squared error: it explains about 0% of the
variance, and it leaves the model's output essentially as it is when the component is off.
"""

READS = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = 0.04  # mean over training rows of this component's activation


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """The activation at this position: the component's mean, whatever the tokens are."""
    return carry, MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Layer 15 MLP down-projection, component 4040: a near-inert, context-driven feature.

What it is: this component reads the layer-15 MLP hidden state mostly through hidden unit
4040 (its input weight is 0.40 on that unit, and the rest is spread thinly), and writes a
small vector into the residual stream. Its activation is roughly 0.26 times that unit's value,
which is positive on Chinese colons, quotes and list separators and on some place names, and
negative on mid-clause Chinese verbs and aspect words. But that unit is itself not predictable
from the current token: a per-token table explains about 1% of this component's activation,
and no concept we could name (script, punctuation, position, a window of Chinese text) explains
more than that. The component's CI is essentially zero everywhere, so switching it off changes
the model's output by almost nothing.

What the program does: it predicts the typical activation (about -0.026, the mean inside a
document) at every token, and 0 at the first token of each document, where the component is
exactly silent. That captures the offset and the silent start; it does not capture the
token-level variation, which is the part the program cannot explain.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

TYPICAL = -0.026  # mean activation inside a document


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    ids = prefix.document_ids
    starts_document = prefix.position == 0 or ids[-1] != ids[-2]
    return carry, (0.0 if starts_document else TYPICAL)

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 4041: a rule-based sketch.

What the component is: one rank-one piece of the MLP down-projection in layer 15. Its
activation is the MLP's hidden vector dotted with one fixed direction (almost all of it
from hidden unit 4041), scaled by that direction's size. Across ordinary text it is a
broad, roughly symmetric signal (std about 0.6, heavy tails) with no single concept behind
it. Token identity, previous-token pairs, script and position together explain only a few
percent of its variance, so this program is a sketch, not a full explanation.

What the program does, using the three facts that stood out:
  1. The first token of each document is silent: it predicts 0.
  2. The second token of each document is, on average, positive: it predicts 0.4.
  3. The 'BS' piece of 'OBSERVATION' in a tool response (the token 'BS' right after 'O')
     is strongly positive: it predicts 4.4.
Everywhere else it predicts 0, near the component's typical value.
"""

READS = ()

FIRST_TOKEN = 0.0
SECOND_TOKEN = 0.4
OBSERVATION_BS = 4.4
ELSEWHERE = 0.0


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # carry: (document label of the last token, how many tokens of that document came before it)
    doc = prefix.document_ids[prefix.position]
    n = carry[1] if carry is not None and carry[0] == doc else 0
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    previous = prefix.token_strings[-2] if n > 0 else ""
    if n == 0:
        value = FIRST_TOKEN
    elif n == 1:
        value = SECOND_TOKEN
    elif token == "BS" and previous == "O":
        value = OBSERVATION_BS
    else:
        value = ELSEWHERE
    return (doc, n + 1), value

"""Layer-15 MLP hidden unit 4042, as seen through this component's direction.

The component reads the layer-15 MLP's hidden units through a direction that is
mostly hidden unit 4042 (about 0.77 of its weight, about half its squared norm),
with smaller weights on a few others (5835, 4808, 2126). Its activation is that
weighted sum, scaled by about 0.95.

What simple concepts can say about it: little. On ordinary text the value is
slightly negative (mean about -0.08) with spread about 0.32, and no word list,
character class, token identity, position or repetition pattern explains more
than a fraction of a percent of the variance. Two things stand out. The first
token of a document is near zero. The blank line that closes an empty think
block at the start of an assistant turn ("<think>" then "\n\n") is strongly
positive, about 1.8, though it is rare.

This program predicts those cases and the ordinary mean everywhere else. It is
a baseline that carries almost none of the component's variance.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

ORDINARY_MEAN = -0.08
DOCUMENT_START = 0.0
THINK_CLOSING_NEWLINE = 1.8


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    t = prefix.position
    if t == 0 or prefix.document_ids[t] != prefix.document_ids[t - 1]:
        return carry, DOCUMENT_START
    if prefix.token_strings[t - 1] == "<think>" and prefix.token_strings[t] == "\n\n":
        return carry, THINK_CLOSING_NEWLINE
    return carry, ORDINARY_MEAN

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj component 4043: a weak, character-class predictor.

The component's activation is a small, diffuse signal (mean about -0.025, standard deviation
about 0.30). Almost none of it is explained by simple features: the current token's class
explains about 0.1% of its variance on held-out text, a whole token-identity table about 2%.
This program predicts the average activation for the class of the newest token: it is a
little lower after newlines and punctuation, and a little higher on CJK and inside
words. Its causal importance is essentially zero, so switching it off barely changes the
model's predictions.
"""

import re
import unicodedata

READS = ()

# Mean activation of the newest token's class, measured on 4096 training rows.
CLASS_MEAN = {
    "newline": -0.049,
    "space": -0.039,
    "punct": -0.040,
    "digit": -0.033,
    "word": -0.031,
    "spaced_word": -0.014,
    "cjk": -0.015,
    "cyrillic": -0.019,
    "other": -0.028,
}


def token_class(text):
    """The class of one token's text, from its characters' Unicode categories."""
    if "�" in text:
        return "other"
    if not text.strip():
        return "newline" if "\n" in text or "\r" in text else "space"
    if re.search(r"[一-鿿]", text):
        return "cjk"
    if re.search(r"[Ѐ-ӿ]", text):
        return "cyrillic"
    if re.fullmatch(r"\s?\d+", text):
        return "digit"
    if re.fullmatch(r"\s?[A-Za-z]+", text):
        return "spaced_word" if text[0] == " " else "word"
    if all(unicodedata.category(c).startswith(("P", "S")) for c in text.strip()):
        return "punct"
    return "other"


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """Predict the class-average activation for the newest token."""
    return carry, CLASS_MEAN[token_class(prefix.token_strings[-1])]

"""Layer-15 MLP neuron 4044 (the down_proj component 4044), as a word-level rule.

The neuron's activation is noisy and mostly unexplained by simple features, but its large
negative values cluster in one place: a content noun that directly follows a preposition,
as in "death" in "cause of death", "birth" in "place of birth" or "sports" in "of sports".
Such words push the neuron negative, strongest after "of". Function words after a
preposition ("of these", "of which") and nouns after other words are about zero. The
program predicts that: a negative value on a noun after a preposition, and zero elsewhere.
"""
from collections.abc import Mapping

import wordnet

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

PREPOSITIONS = {
    "of", "in", "for", "on", "to", "with", "at", "from", "by", "de", "di", "per",
    "about", "into", "over", "under", "between",
}


def is_noun(token: str) -> bool:
    """A whole, alphabetic, space-led word that WordNet lists as a noun."""
    word = token.strip()
    return (
        token.startswith(" ")
        and word.isalpha()
        and "noun" in wordnet.parts_of_speech(word.lower())
    )


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    if prefix.position == 0 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]:
        return carry, 0.0
    before = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip()
    if before not in PREPOSITIONS:
        return carry, 0.0
    noun = is_noun(prefix.token_strings[-1])
    if before == "of":
        return carry, -0.9 if noun else -0.1
    return carry, -0.3 if noun else -0.1

"""Partitive "of" detector (plus Romance "de" / "di").

Component p-82af68dd@100000/layers.15.mlp.down_proj:4045 fires on the word "of" when
the "of" introduces a part or a quantity of something: "some of", "most of", "one of",
"all of", "majority of", "percent of", "the number of". It is strongest right after a
quantifier or a fraction word, weaker when the word before "of" selects "of" as a fixed
phrase ("instance of", "because of", "out of", "capable of"), and about zero on every
other token. "de" and "di" (Spanish, French, Italian, Portuguese "of") get a small value.

What the program leaves out: on ordinary tokens the component sits in a diffuse
background of about +/-0.5 that no word or context rule explains; that is most of the
unexplained variance.
"""

READS = ()  # reads no other component

# Quantifiers and fraction/quantity words that take a partitive "of".
QUANTITY_WORDS = {
    "all", "some", "most", "many", "few", "several", "none", "each", "any", "both",
    "either", "neither", "half", "much", "more", "one", "two", "three", "four", "five",
    "six", "seven", "eight", "nine", "ten", "majority", "minority", "percent",
    "percentage", "portion", "fraction", "proportion", "rest", "remainder", "bulk",
}

# Words that take a fixed "of" of their own (no partitive reading).
FIXED_OF_WORDS = {
    "instance", "out", "because", "instead", "terms", "care", "way", "aware", "capable",
    "consist", "consists", "kind", "sort", "type", "rid", "guilty", "full", "afraid",
    "member", "cause", "due", "regardless", "favor", "independent",
}

PARTITIVE_OF = 7.0  # "of" after a quantity word
PLAIN_OF = 4.0      # any other "of"
FIXED_OF = 1.8      # "of" that a word selects
ROMANCE_OF = 1.5    # "de" / "di"


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    same_document = len(prefix.document_ids) > 1 and (
        prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
    )
    before = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip().lower() if same_document else ""
    if token == "of":
        if before in QUANTITY_WORDS:
            value = PARTITIVE_OF
        elif before in FIXED_OF_WORDS:
            value = FIXED_OF
        else:
            value = PLAIN_OF
    elif token in ("de", "di"):
        value = ROMANCE_OF
    else:
        value = 0.0
    return carry, value


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # A quick look: the value at each token of a short sentence.
    class Prefix:
        def __init__(self, tokens):
            self.token_strings = tokens
            self.document_ids = [0] * len(tokens)

    sentence = "Most of the students left because of rain, one of them said.".split(" ")
    tokens = [" " + w if i else w for i, w in enumerate(sentence)]
    carry = None
    for i in range(len(tokens)):
        carry, value = step(carry, Prefix(tokens[: i + 1]), {})
        print(f"{tokens[i]!r:14} {value}")

"""Predicts the component's activation from the current word alone.

The component's input direction is about half MLP hidden unit 4046 of layer 15 (weight 0.6
on that unit, at most 0.06 on any other). That unit runs high on words that open a
condition, comparison, or check in reasoning text: "not", "than", "whether", "if",
"ensure", "exactly", "at least", "less/greater", "equal", "within", "check", "cannot",
and symbols like ">" and "!=". On those words the activation averages about 0.17; on
other words it averages about 0.03, with large scatter that no word list predicts.

So the program predicts 0.17 on those words and 0.03 elsewhere. On eval it explains about
0.2% of the variance. Most of its activation is not explained by the current word or by
the words just before it.
"""

READS = ()

CONDITION_WORDS = frozenset(
    "not than whether if ensure sure exactly least within greater less equal check "
    "cannot match contains exist provide must verify > >= ≥ != ".split()
)
"""Words (lowercased, without the leading space) that introduce a condition or comparison."""

ON_VALUE = 0.17
"""Average activation on those words."""

OFF_VALUE = 0.03
"""Average activation on all other words."""


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    return None, ON_VALUE if word in CONDITION_WORDS else OFF_VALUE

"""Layer 15 MLP hidden unit 4047's component (down_proj component 4047), as a word rule.

What it does: this component reads mostly one MLP hidden unit (about half of its input
direction), and that unit is sparse and context-dependent. Its activation is positive on
words that bring up an alternative or a method ("Alternatively", "approach", "another",
"method", "embodiment", "invention") and negative on hedging and second-thought words
("maybe", "perhaps", "however", "instead", "actually", "wait"). Everywhere else it is near
zero. The rule predicts the average activation of each group, on the current token only.

It explains very little: on the eval rows it captures about 0.15% of the activation's
variance (correlation 0.04), and its edit leaves the model's output essentially where
switching the component off does. A per-token table of mean activations does only a little
better on held-out training rows (about 0.5% of variance), so token identity is not where
this component's variance lives.

The component writes a 'a closing quotation mark is coming' signal into the residual
stream. It sits near zero on most tokens. What moves it is a few kinds of token:

* Strongly positive (about +16): the conversion letter of a printf-style format
  specifier: the `s` of `%s`, the `d` of `%d`, the `f` of `%.2f`, and so on. Inside a
  format string a closing quote is about to follow.
* Moderately positive (about +6): a format placeholder, `{}` or `{:.2f}`.
* Negative (about -5): an opening quotation mark that starts speech right after a
  sentence end (`... they said. “`). A quote has just opened, so no closing quote is
  due yet. A full-width colon or comma followed by an opening quote (`：“`, `，“`)
  gives about -4.5.

+/-0.5 background, so this explains only part of the variance.

PLACEHOLDERS = {"{}", " {}", " {:"}
OPEN_QUOTES = {" “", ' "'}
FULLWIDTH_OPEN = {"：“", "，“"}
SENTENCE_END = {".", "!", "?"}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    cur = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2] if len(prefix.token_strings) > 1 else ""
    recent = prefix.token_strings[-4:-1]
    if len(prefix.document_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] != prefix.document_ids[-1]:

    if len(cur) == 1 and cur in CONVERSIONS and any("%" in s for s in recent):
        return carry, 16.0
    if cur in PLACEHOLDERS:
        return carry, 6.0
    if cur in FULLWIDTH_OPEN:
        return carry, -4.5
    if cur in OPEN_QUOTES and prev[-1:] in SENTENCE_END:
        return carry, -5.0
    return carry, 0.0

  `using`, `namespace` or `#include`): the `public` of `public class Foo`. Strongest, about -44.

- `import`, `namespace`, `package`/`using`/`use` at the start of a line: about -8, -13, -4.
- the `.util` piece of `import java.util...`: about -9.
- an indented ` public` inside a class body: about -5.
- a Python docstring opener (the triple-quote token after indentation): a small positive, +12.

HEADERS = {"import", "package", "using", "namespace", "#include"}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # carry: (document id, whether this document has shown a file header yet)
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    seen = carry[1] if carry and carry[0] == doc else False
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2] if prefix.position > 0 else "\n"
    column0 = prev.endswith("\n") or prev == "<|endoftext|>" or prefix.position == 0
    indented = prev.strip() == "" and not column0

    if column0 and tok == "public":

    elif tok in (" public", "\tpublic") and (column0 or indented):
        value = -5.0
    elif column0 and tok == "import":

    elif column0 and tok == "namespace":
        value = -13.0
    elif column0 and tok in ("package", "using", "use"):

    elif tok == ".util":
        value = -9.0
    elif tok == ' ' + '"' * 3 and indented:

    return (doc, seen), value

    "abbreviation acronym synonym nickname alias phrase phrases terminology referred".split()

ON_WORD = -0.4

a dense, context-driven neuron. Token identity, the neighbouring token, document position and
linear token-context features each explain about 1% of its variance or less. Its large values
(|x| > 3) are enriched on digits (about 3.5 times their base rate, most of all the digit 0) and

50/50. So the program predicts only each character class's small mean, and 0 at a document's
first token, where the component is always 0. Means are from 4096 training rows.

import re

READS = ()

CLASS_MEAN = {
    "digit": 0.045,
    "punct": 0.034,
    "newline": 0.027,
    "word": 0.028,
    "mixed": 0.028,
    "cjk": 0.002,
    "space": -0.004,
    "word_sp": -0.010,
}


def kind(text):
    if text.strip() == "":
        return "space"
    if "\n" in text or "\r" in text:
        return "newline"
    if re.fullmatch(r"\s*\d+", text):
        return "digit"
    if re.search(r"[一-鿿぀-ヿ]", text):
        return "cjk"
    if re.fullmatch(r"\s*[A-Za-z]+", text):
        return "word_sp" if text.startswith(" ") else "word"

    return "mixed"

    if len(prefix.token_ids) == 1 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]:

    return carry, CLASS_MEAN[kind(prefix.token_strings[-1])]

everywhere else. Colons that open a Python/shell block ("try:", "do", "else:") stay
near zero. Other tokens carry only small, context-dependent noise, which this program
does not model.

BLOCK_WORDS = {
    "if", "elif", "else", "try", "except", "finally", "for", "while",
    "def", "class", "with", "do", "then", "case", "default",

    # carry: the words typed so far on the current line, within one document.

"""Layer-15 MLP unit 4082 (the component's write-in direction), as a rhetorical-phase reader.

What the component is: nearly all of its activation is one hidden unit of layer 15's MLP
(unit 4082 carries about half the variance by itself). It is quiet in ordinary text and
large inside scientific and biomedical abstracts, where it is positive while the writing
sets up the background (what is known, prior studies, an open gap) and negative once the
writing turns to the study itself (its aims, methods, results, conclusions).

How this program mimics it: it reads the words so far, one token at a time, and keeps two
running tallies that reset at each new document:
  phase   - decaying count of background cue words (+1) minus study/results cue words (-1);
  science - decaying count of scientific-register words, a gate that is near 0 in
            everyday text and high inside research prose.
It predicts  a * phase + b * phase * science + c * science.
The coefficients were least-squares fits on training rows; the word lists are hand-picked.
"""

READS = ()  # reads no other component

DECAY_PHASE = 0.8  # how fast the background/study tally forgets
DECAY_SCIENCE = 0.98  # how fast the scientific-register gate forgets

BACKGROUND = {  # framing the field and the gap: positive
    "however", "despite", "although", "previous", "previously", "reported", "studies",
    "known", "unknown", "remains", "limited", "little", "recently", "evidence", "has",
    "have", "been", "often", "several", "whether", "hypothesized",
}
STUDY = {  # the present work: its aims, methods, results, conclusions: negative
    "we", "our", "study", "here", "aim", "aimed", "objective", "objectives", "methods",
    "results", "showed", "found", "conclusion", "conclusions", "were", "was", "obtained",
    "calculated", "analysis", "data", "significantly", "patients", "participants", "groups",
    "used", "this",
}
SCIENCE = {  # words that mark research prose
    "study", "patients", "results", "analysis", "significantly", "cells", "mice", "clinical",
    "disease", "treatment", "expression", "groups", "methods", "data", "showed", "cancer",
    "risk", "children", "levels", "associated", "gene", "protein", "effects", "subjects",
    "trial", "therapy", "outcome", "efficacy", "increased", "decreased", "compared",
    "participants", "samples", "tissue", "rats",
}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    new_document = (
        carry is None
        or len(prefix.document_ids) < 2
        or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    )
    phase, science = (0.0, 0.0) if new_document else carry
    cue = (word in BACKGROUND) - (word in STUDY)
    phase = DECAY_PHASE * phase + cue
    science = DECAY_SCIENCE * science + (word in SCIENCE)
    value = 0.028 * phase + 0.169 * phase * science + 0.021 * science
    return (phase, science), float(value)

"""Layer 15 MLP hidden unit 4083 (its down_proj component), read off the tokens.

What it does: this component is one MLP hidden unit of layer 15 written out
through its down projection. Its activation is near zero or slightly negative
on most text, with rare large positive spikes. The spikes come in
step-by-step reasoning and maths working: the end-of-thinking tag </think>
(the biggest), the multiplication sign and other operators inside a
calculation, and reasoning transition words such as "Wait", "Alternatively"
and "Hmm". Ordinary prose, names, code and Chinese text sit slightly below zero.

This program predicts the activation from the newest token alone, using a
few word classes with the mean activation measured for each on training text.
It does not model the slow, local drift that carries most of the remaining
variance, so it explains only a sliver of it.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

END_OF_THINKING = {"</think>"}
REASONING_WORDS = {
    "Wait", "Alternatively", "Hmm", "Oh", "Ah", "However", "Although",
    "Well", "Another", "Note", "While", "Let", "Given", "Looking",
    "Actually", "Okay",
}
MATH_SYMBOLS = {"×", "*", "^", "=", "√", "sqrt", "³", "²", "+", "(", "/"}
DIGITS = set("0123456789")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    # A document's first token: the activation is about zero there.
    if len(prefix.token_ids) == 1 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]:
        return carry, 0.0
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip()
    if word in END_OF_THINKING:
        value = 2.2
    elif word in REASONING_WORDS:
        value = 0.5
    elif word in MATH_SYMBOLS:
        value = 0.1
    elif word and all(ch in DIGITS for ch in word):
        value = -0.04
    else:
        value = -0.06
    return carry, value

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 4084: a clause-position tilt (explains almost nothing).

What the component does, as far as a person can read it: its activation is mostly driven
by MLP hidden unit 4084 of layer 15, a diffuse feature with a heavy positive tail. Its
largest values come where a main clause begins after a fronted conditional or temporal
clause ("If a suitable agreement can't be reached[,] you may wind up ...", "after leaving a
card[,] they [will] return ..."). The commas that close such a clause and the first few
words of the main clause are enriched for large values.

This program encodes only that tilt: it tracks each sentence's opening word, and
predicts a small positive value on the comma that closes a sentence-initial
subordinator clause (if, when, after, since, ...) and on the first five words after it.
Everything else gets 0. It is a readable description of the top examples, not a good
predictor: on held-out rows it explains about 0% of the activation's variance (see the
submission explanation). Token identity, previous token, position, script and
sentence position were all tested and explain no variance either.
"""

READS = ()

# Words that open a fronted subordinate (conditional, temporal or causal) clause.
SUBORDINATORS = {
    "if", "when", "after", "since", "once", "although", "because", "unless",
    "before", "though", "whenever", "until", "while",
}
# Tokens that end a sentence.
SENTENCE_END = set(".!?\n")

# Values predicted at each kind of position (typical activations at those spots).
SUBORDINATOR_WORD = 0.05  # the opening subordinator itself
CLAUSE_COMMA = 0.3  # the comma that closes the fronted clause
MAIN_CLAUSE_START = 0.2  # the first five tokens of the main clause after it
MAIN_CLAUSE_LENGTH = 5


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """Run once per token. carry = (state, tokens seen in the main clause so far)."""
    state, seen = carry if carry else ("start", 0)
    if prefix.position == 0 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]:
        state, seen = "start", 0  # a new document starts a new sentence

    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    word = token.strip().lower()
    value = 0.0
    if any(ch in SENTENCE_END for ch in token):
        state, seen = "start", 0
    elif state == "start" and word in SUBORDINATORS:
        state, value = "subordinate", SUBORDINATOR_WORD
    elif state == "start":
        state = "other"  # sentence opens with something else
    elif state == "subordinate" and "," in token:
        state, seen, value = "main", 0, CLAUSE_COMMA
    elif state == "main" and seen < MAIN_CLAUSE_LENGTH:
        seen += 1
        value = MAIN_CLAUSE_START
    return (state, seen), value

the noun or adjective that takes a complement naming what it affects, causes or
relates to ("effects", "impact", "result", "consequences", "related", "sensitive",

("the effects of", "impact of", "consequences of", "related to", "response to").
Plain "of" and "to" elsewhere are mildly negative. Everything else sits near zero.

The values are the average activation in each group, measured on training text.
Most of the component's variance is diffuse and not explained by any word
concept, so this program explains only a sliver of it.

    "consequence", "consequences", "implication", "implications",

    "reaction", "reactions", "adapt", "due", "caused", "associated", "reflect", "reflects",

def _word(text):

def step(carry, prefix, upstream):

What it is: the component's activation is (hidden @ V_c) * |U_c|, a dense weighted sum over
all 6144 MLP hidden units. Its largest single weight is hidden unit 4086 (about 16% of its
variance), which is itself most negative on chat and reasoning markers such as "</think>",
"<think>", "<tool_call>" and "<|im_end|>". Across tokens the activation has no compact
pattern: token identity, token class, previous token and position in the document together
explain well under 1% of its variance on held-out text.

What this program does: it predicts the few things that are visible at the token level:
  - reasoning-block markers ("<think>", "</think>") push the activation clearly negative;
  - whitespace-only tokens push it slightly negative;
  - everything else is predicted as 0, the component's typical value.

"""

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

THINK_MARKERS = frozenset({"<think>", "</think>"})

WHITESPACE_VALUE = -0.05  # the mean over whitespace-only tokens is about -0.06

"""Decimal-point detector for numbers in running text.

The component fires on the '.' that follows a digit, i.e. the point in
'4.0', '$3.99', '6.25 s', 'version 2.0', '0.5'. It fires strongly (about 2)
when the number sits inside a line of text. When the digit starts a line,
as in list numbering ('3. Next step'), it fires only weakly. Everything else,
including commas and colons in numbers and all letters, gives 0.
"""

READS = ()

MID_LINE = 2.2  # decimal point inside a line of text
LINE_START = 0.5  # digit that begins a line, e.g. list numbering


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    toks = prefix.token_strings
    docs = prefix.document_ids
    # the previous token must exist and belong to the same document
    if len(toks) < 2 or docs[-2] != docs[-1]:
        return carry, 0.0
    if toks[-1] != "." or not toks[-2].strip().isdigit():
        return carry, 0.0
    # is the digit the first thing on its line?
    before = toks[-3] if len(toks) >= 3 and docs[-3] == docs[-1] else "\n"
    line_start = "\n" in before
    return carry, LINE_START if line_start else MID_LINE

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 4088: a weak, mostly unexplained readout.

What it does: its activation is essentially a linear readout of layer 15's MLP hidden
units (its V vector is dominated by hidden unit 4088 itself, and the rest is spread over
thousands of units). Across the training text that readout is not tied to any token,
character class, repeated n-gram or context word: token identity explains about 2% of its
variance, and even a lookup of the previous activations explains under 6%.

The one regularity we can state simply: it is larger just after a document starts and
fades with distance into the document. So this program predicts zero at a document's first
token and, after that, a value that falls off as 1/log2(position + 1) from about 0.16 at
the second token to about 0.03 by position 64, and about 0.02 (the mean) far in.

It explains very little (about 0.2% of variance on held-out rows). A token lookup table
would explain about 2%, but it would be a table of arbitrary token ids with no concept
behind it, so it is not used here.
"""

import math

READS = ()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        pos = 0  # first token of a document
    else:
        pos = carry[1] + 1
    if pos == 0:
        value = 0.0
    else:
        value = 0.167 / math.log2(pos + 1) - 0.003
    return (doc, pos), value

"""Predicts down_proj component 4093 of layer 15 (p-82af68dd@100000).

What the component is: its input direction is mostly MLP hidden unit 4093 of layer 15
(0.90 of its norm 1.07), so its activation is roughly that unit's value times a constant. Most of the time it is small and diffuse (std about 0.4). Its strongest
negative values (-5 to -19) fall on words inside a clause that opens with a verb-ing
word at the start of a sentence, e.g. "Having an experienced attorney [by] your side",
"Understanding the [latest] trends", "Getting into a reputable treatment [center]".

What this program does: after a sentence-initial verb-ing word (a gerund or participle,
checked with WordNet), it predicts a mean shift of -0.2 for the next few tokens, until
punctuation or a newline ends the clause. It predicts 0 everywhere else. The sign is not
consistent inside these clauses ("Making this problem [more]" is strongly positive), so
this captures only the average shift, which explains very little of the variance.
"""

import regex
import wordnet

READS = ()

GERUND = regex.compile(r" ?[A-Za-z]+ing")
SENTENCE_END = regex.compile(r'[.!?:;"“”\n]\s*$')
CLAUSE_BREAK = regex.compile(r"[\p{P}\n]")
MAX_DISTANCE = 6
SHIFT = -0.2


def is_verb_ing(token):
    """A word ending in -ing that WordNet lists as a verb ("Having", not "something")."""
    return bool(GERUND.fullmatch(token)) and "verb" in wordnet.parts_of_speech(token.strip().lower())


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    tokens, docs = prefix.token_strings, prefix.document_ids
    now = len(tokens) - 1
    for distance in range(1, MAX_DISTANCE + 1):
        start = now - distance
        if start < 0 or docs[start] != docs[now]:
            break
        if not is_verb_ing(tokens[start]):
            continue
        opens_sentence = start == 0 or docs[start - 1] != docs[start] or bool(
            SENTENCE_END.search(tokens[start - 1])
        )
        if not opens_sentence:
            continue
        if any(CLAUSE_BREAK.search(tokens[j]) for j in range(start + 1, now)):
            continue
        return carry, SHIFT
    return carry, 0.0
